package_info.package_name: Gootkit loader (Gootloader) campaign abusing VLC Media Player
package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via ZIP archive, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (malware campaign, not a versioned package)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire campaign is malicious because it orchestrates a multi-stage malware infection chain. It leverages SEO poisoning to lure victims to download a ZIP archive containing a JavaScript file, which, when executed, initiates a sequence of actions: dropping and running a PowerShell script, downloading a trojanized VLC Media Player executable (msdtc.exe) and a malicious DLL (libvlc.dll), and sideloading the DLL to establish a Cobalt Strike beacon for remote command and control, lateral movement, and credential theft. The campaign abuses trusted software and file names to evade detection and facilitate post-exploitation activities.

execution_context.trigger: user-execution (runtime, after opening JS file from ZIP)
execution_context.file_location: JavaScript file inside ZIP archive (initial infection vector, typically masquerading as a document template)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The JavaScript file, when executed, writes a PowerShell script (e.g., soo.ps1) to disk and then executes it using the Windows Script Host. The PowerShell script is responsible for downloading additional payloads from a remote server.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after user execution, the JavaScript file writes a PowerShell script to disk and executes it, initiating a download of further malware from a remote server, resulting in the next stage of the infection chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: JavaScript files delivered via ZIP archives that write and execute PowerShell scripts are a common initial access technique in malware campaigns, enabling the attacker to bypass email and web filters and deliver further payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate JavaScript files, especially those masquerading as document templates, should not write and execute PowerShell scripts or initiate network connections to download additional code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated deployment or installer scripts may use similar techniques, but only when sourced from trusted, verified vendors and with user awareness.
key_indicators: JavaScript file in ZIP archive initiates PowerShell execution
Writes PowerShell script (e.g., soo.ps1) to disk
Executes PowerShell via Windows Script Host
Downloads further payloads from remote server

execution_context.trigger: PowerShell execution (runtime, after JS file runs)
execution_context.file_location: Dropped PowerShell script (e.g., soo.ps1, PSHound.ps1) in user or temp directory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The PowerShell script downloads msdtc.exe (a trojanized VLC Media Player executable) and libvlc.dll (malicious DLL) from a remote server, writes them to disk in the same directory, and then executes msdtc.exe.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after being invoked by the JavaScript file, the PowerShell script downloads msdtc.exe and libvlc.dll from a remote server, writes them to disk, and executes msdtc.exe, which loads the malicious DLL to initiate Cobalt Strike beaconing.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: PowerShell scripts that download and execute unsigned executables and DLLs from untrusted sources are a hallmark of malware delivery, enabling attackers to introduce arbitrary code onto the system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PowerShell scripts should not download and execute binaries or DLLs from untrusted or unknown sources, nor should they place files in user or temp directories for execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise deployment scripts may download and install software, but only from trusted, signed sources and with proper user notification.
key_indicators: PowerShell script downloads msdtc.exe and libvlc.dll
Writes executables and DLLs to disk in user-accessible directories
File names mimic legitimate software (msdtc.exe, libvlc.dll)

execution_context.trigger: DLL sideloading (runtime, when msdtc.exe is executed)
execution_context.file_location: libvlc.dll (malicious DLL placed alongside msdtc.exe in user or temp directory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The malicious libvlc.dll (detected as Trojan.Win64.COBEACON.SWG) is loaded by msdtc.exe (a trojanized VLC Media Player), which then initiates a Cobalt Strike beacon to a remote command and control server.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when msdtc.exe is executed, it loads the malicious libvlc.dll via DLL sideloading, which establishes a Cobalt Strike beacon, enabling remote command and control, lateral movement, and credential theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DLL sideloading with a malicious DLL is a well-known technique for malware persistence and evasion, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code within the context of a trusted process.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate VLC installations should not have a trojanized libvlc.dll; DLLs loaded by VLC should not initiate outbound C2 communications or process injection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: DLL sideloading is used in legitimate plugin architectures, but not for establishing C2 beacons or launching post-exploitation frameworks.
key_indicators: libvlc.dll is not the original, but a trojanized version
DLL initiates Cobalt Strike beaconing upon load
DLL loaded by msdtc.exe (masquerading as VLC Media Player)
Outbound network connections to C2 infrastructure from msdtc.exe

execution_context.trigger: post-exploitation (runtime, after Cobalt Strike beacon established)
execution_context.file_location: PSHound.ps1 (SharpHound PowerShell script), executed via Cobalt Strike in user or temp directory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: PSHound.ps1 (SharpHound) is executed to enumerate Active Directory objects and perform internal network reconnaissance, collecting credentials and mapping the domain for lateral movement.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the Cobalt Strike beacon is established, PSHound.ps1 is executed to scan the internal network, enumerate Active Directory objects, and collect credentials, facilitating lateral movement and privilege escalation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Execution of SharpHound/PSHound is a known post-exploitation technique for Active Directory enumeration, commonly used by attackers to map internal networks and identify targets for lateral movement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal user activity should not involve running AD enumeration scripts or performing network scans to LDAP/SMB ports.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red team assessments or IT security audits may use SharpHound, but such activity is not expected in standard user workflows and should be tightly controlled.
key_indicators: Execution of PSHound.ps1 or SharpHound PowerShell scripts
Network scans to LDAP (389), SMB (445), and Global Catalog (3268) ports
Enumeration of Active Directory objects from user or temp directories

attack_chain.action: Victim visits SEO-poisoned website and downloads a ZIP archive containing a JavaScript file masquerading as a document template.
User executes the JavaScript file, which writes and runs a PowerShell script.
attack_chain.leads_to: PowerShell script downloads and executes trojanized VLC components

attack_chain.action: PowerShell script downloads msdtc.exe (trojanized VLC) and malicious libvlc.dll, writes them to disk, and executes msdtc.exe.
msdtc.exe (VLC) sideloads libvlc.dll, which launches a Cobalt Strike beacon to a remote C2 server.
Cobalt Strike beacon executes PSHound.ps1 for Active Directory enumeration and internal network reconnaissance.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential theft, lateral movement, and potential deployment of further payloads

behavioral_signatures: Execution of JavaScript files from ZIP archives that write and execute PowerShell scripts
PowerShell scripts downloading and executing binaries or DLLs from untrusted remote servers
DLL sideloading where libvlc.dll is loaded by msdtc.exe or VLC Media Player from non-standard locations
Outbound network connections consistent with Cobalt Strike beaconing patterns
Execution of SharpHound/PSHound PowerShell scripts for Active Directory enumeration
Network scans to internal LDAP (389), SMB (445), and Global Catalog (3268) ports originating from user endpoints
file_indicators: ZIP archives containing JavaScript files masquerading as document templates
Presence of msdtc.exe in user download or temp directories, especially if not signed by Microsoft
libvlc.dll present alongside msdtc.exe, with hash not matching official VLC releases
PSHound.ps1 or soo.ps1 scripts found in user or temp directories
Unusual creation or execution of files in user-accessible directories
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known or suspected Cobalt Strike C2 infrastructure
Network scans to internal ports 389 (LDAP), 445 (SMB), and 3268 (Global Catalog)
Connections to domains or IP addresses associated with Gootkit loader campaigns as identified in threat intelligence feeds
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of JavaScript files from ZIP archives that invoke PowerShell, particularly when the PowerShell script downloads and executes binaries or DLLs from remote servers. Flag DLL sideloading events where libvlc.dll is loaded by msdtc.exe or VLC Media Player from non-standard or user directories. Detect Cobalt Strike beaconing patterns in outbound network traffic, including periodic connections to suspicious domains or IPs. Alert on execution of SharpHound/PSHound scripts and on network scans to LDAP/SMB/Global Catalog ports from user endpoints. Scan for the presence of suspicious files (msdtc.exe, libvlc.dll, PSHound.ps1, soo.ps1) in user or temp directories, and verify file hashes against known-good versions.
